claims.claim_text: The Microchip PIC 16C84, released in 1993, was the first microcontroller that was neither UV-erasable nor one-time-programmable: it stored its program in EEPROM, which allowed the part to be reprogrammed in circuit without a UV eraser or an expensive in-circuit emulator that emulated the whole chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was the first microcontroller that wasn't either UV erasable or one time programmable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Solar Cells, SparkFun, TSMC - The Detroit Debunking

claims.claim_text: Microchip became the de facto standard in the hobbyist world because it was first to combine a reprogrammable microcontroller with a programmer cheap enough to build at home or hang off a PC serial port; competing vendors of the era sold development tools costing several thousand dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: because they were the first to introduce reprogrammable microcontrollers with a cheap hobbyist programming interface
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: In the 1990s a development kit for a PIC microcontroller could cost a couple of thousand dollars and was sold only through dealers to account-holding businesses, so an individual could not simply buy one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was a couple of thousand dollars to buy a dev kit for a PIC microcontroller
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Microchip began as an EEPROM memory maker losing money in a commodity market, and turned itself around by applying its EEPROM process to the PIC architecture to create field-programmable microcontrollers; previously a customer sent code to Motorola for a mask-programmed part and waited roughly sixteen weeks, by which time the code had usually changed.
claims.quote_verbatim: we applied our EEPROM technology to the microcontroller architecture to make the field programmable microcontrollers
claims.speaker: Steve Sanghi
claims.episode_title: Steve Sanghi - Microchip CEO for 31 Years!

claims.claim_text: Microcontrollers grew by accretion of peripherals: the earliest parts were a core with I/O ports and internal memory, to which serial ports, UARTs and analogue-to-digital converters were progressively added until the modern part includes nearly everything.
claims.quote_verbatim: They started out, they were just a microcontroller with IO ports and some internal memory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Op amps, Microchips & Mergers - Narquois Nerd Nescience - Narquois Nerd Nescience

claims.claim_text: Integrated UARTs became universal roughly twenty to twenty-five years ago; before that a design needed an external UART chip, and that integration marks the practical divide between the microprocessor and the microcontroller.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's the, it's the microprocessor versus microcontroller. That's really when that sort of happened
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: LEDs and EVs with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: By the early 2000s the BASIC Stamp cost more than one hundred dollars once imported into Europe with tariffs, which discouraged students from experimenting for fear of destroying the board; Arduino was targeted at roughly twenty euros, about the price of a pizza and a beer, precisely to make destroying one inconsequential.
claims.quote_verbatim: you ended up spending more than $100 for a microcontroller
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: The traditional definition of a microcontroller is a part that holds all of its memory internally, both program and data, so that it can be programmed and can execute with no external chips; a device that must fetch its program from an external memory is by that definition a microprocessor, regardless of whether the interface is a parallel bus or SPI.
claims.quote_verbatim: the definition of microcontroller is that it can all you can program it and executes with no external chips
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Embedded Flash requires additional and different process steps from plain logic, so leaving Flash off the die lowers silicon cost; specialist Flash vendors make the memory more cheaply than a microcontroller vendor can integrate it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it does make the silicon cheaper if you don't have to build the Flash process into your silicon
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Practitioners increasingly define a microcontroller by its design intent rather than its memory map: high integration, low cost, low cross-system latency and a focus on I/O and hard real-time behaviour rather than processing throughput, with integration pursued because it is cheaper. On that view a flashless part is still a microcontroller, and whether Flash belongs on the die is simply a cost question.
claims.quote_verbatim: I would say this is a flashless microcontroller
claims.speaker: Luke Renn
claims.episode_title: Embedded Hardware with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: The RP2040 carries 264 KB of on-chip SRAM but no internal Flash, supporting up to 16 MB of external Flash over a QSPI bus; embedding Flash would have required extra mask steps, and it was omitted to hold the die cost down.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's got 264k of on chip sram
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The RP2040 was designed from a clean sheet by engineers whose background was in large SoCs rather than microcontrollers, with goals of very low cost on a fairly modern process node and deterministic behaviour that a programmer could reason about; the first generation deliberately omitted security features and gave little attention to power consumption, so its deep sleep modes are not competitive.
claims.quote_verbatim: We were trying to design a microcontroller sort of almost with a blank sheet of paper
claims.speaker: James Adams
claims.episode_title: The RP2350 with the Raspberry Pi Team

claims.claim_text: The RP2350 adds a built-in switching regulator that steps 3.3 V down to the core supply using an external inductor and capacitors, and pairs two Cortex-M33 cores with two RISC-V cores.
claims.quote_verbatim: one of the things this new microcontroller has is a built-in switching regulator
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Bus fabric choice separates a microcontroller from a peripheral-hub chip: the RP2040's small fabric reads a peripheral in one or two clock cycles for low latency, whereas a PCI Express-connected fabric feeding busmasters such as USB, cameras and displays trades latency of around ten cycles for throughput.
claims.quote_verbatim: So if you want to go and read a peripheral, that will take one or two clock cycles on RP2040
claims.speaker: Liam Fraser
claims.episode_title: The RP1 and beyond with the Raspberry Pi Hardware team

claims.claim_text: A fifty-cent microcontroller arrives already packaged, tested and documented with a data sheet available to everyone, which is the economic barrier any custom-silicon alternative has to clear.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can buy a 50-cent microcontroller that's already packaged, tested, and has a complete data sheet
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Carnassial Chip Chemicals

claims.claim_text: At consumer volumes of hundreds of thousands of units, a small ARM part such as an STM32 can be bought for around a quarter and other processors for under ten cents.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get that one for like a quarter, and there are lots of other processors you can get for like under $0.10
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: The cheapest conventional 8-bit parts, such as a PIC in a SOT-23-6 package, sit around thirty to forty cents; a three-cent microcontroller is an order of magnitude below that, and the difference only repays learning a new platform well into hundreds of thousands of units.
claims.quote_verbatim: Unless you're up into like well into the 100Ks, it doesn't really matter if your micro is 3 cents or 8 cents
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: For a one-off or a build of ten to a hundred units the microcontroller price is irrelevant, so the rational choice is the most familiar and best-tooled part rather than the cheapest.
claims.quote_verbatim: It doesn't matter whether or not you pay three cents for a micro or 30 cents or even $3 for a micro
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Within a microcontroller family the price step for memory is disproportionate: an otherwise identical part with 128 KB instead of 32 KB costs considerably more because memory occupies a large fraction of the die area.
claims.quote_verbatim: Between a part that has more memory. It's exactly the same part. But it's 128k instead of 32k for example
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A single distributor can list on the order of eighty thousand microcontroller part numbers, many of them the same die in different packages, which makes vendor-neutral tutorial material for any specific part commercially unattractive to produce.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's something like 80,000 part numbers on DigiKey for microcontrollers
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Renesas has been the world's largest microcontroller manufacturer by volume, ahead of Microchip, Atmel and Texas Instruments, on the strength of very large design wins rather than hobbyist visibility.
claims.quote_verbatim: This is the world's biggest microcontroller manufacturer
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Renesas volume comes from white goods and automotive rather than from the maker or consultancy market, where a domestic appliance typically contains one of its 8-bit or low-cost 32-bit parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: every fridge has, you know, one of their 8-bitters in it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: We're Sorry! But Apple Ain't! - Remorseless RAM Racketeering

claims.claim_text: Microchip began an analogue products group around 1998 on the reasoning that customers designing in a PIC also needed op amps, brownout reset circuits, supervisors and regulators, and that the company already ran the mixed-signal processes required. Microcontrollers now account for roughly half of the company's revenue, the remainder coming from analogue, FPGAs and interface controllers acquired with companies such as Microsemi and, through it, Actel.
claims.quote_verbatim: roughly microcontrollers are about half of microchips total revenue
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: 32-bit microcontrollers are not available in the very small packages 8-bit parts occupy: they carry large memories and complex peripherals, so they are physically larger and require substantially more initialisation code before they will do anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: go out and try and buy an 8-pin, a tiny 8-pin 32-bit micro. You can't
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Apple HQ and Vintage Arcade Games - The Mothership Manifesto

claims.claim_text: The case for 8-bit parts is power and resource proportionality rather than cost alone: an application that uses a million transistors should not have to power up a hundred million. Where a product is not price sensitive, however, Cortex-M parts have become cheap and capable enough that choosing an 8-bitter is hard to justify.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't want to power up 100 million transistors when you're only using a million
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle

claims.claim_text: Peripheral fit, not core width, often decides the part: an 8051-based part such as the EFM8 can win a socket purely because its peripheral set matches the hardware, even where the processing requirement would be met by anything.
claims.quote_verbatim: The only reason I chose it, it's got an 8051 in it, is because of the peripherals
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Legacy cores such as the 6502 and 8051 persist in new silicon because they are royalty-free: the 6502's patents expired and Intel placed the 8051 in the public domain, whereas embedding an ARM core costs the chipmaker either a per-unit royalty or a fixed fee negotiated up front. This is why inexpensive display and touchscreen controllers still ship with 8051 cores.
claims.quote_verbatim: is that these cores are free
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: The 8051 supports fast context switching in hardware through four register banks: a task is assigned a bank, and switching context means telling the core which bank is live rather than pushing and popping the entire machine state onto a stack as a conventional CPU must.
claims.quote_verbatim: Because you have a sign that this routine is using bank one
claims.speaker: Vincent Himpe
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Vincent Himpe - Escaped Electron Elocution

claims.claim_text: RISC-V cores are offered in distinct microcontroller and application-processor classes; an MCU-class RISC-V core can be positioned between a Cortex-M4 and a Cortex-M7 in compute. The instruction set's extensibility allows custom instructions to be offloaded to on-chip FPGA fabric to accelerate operations such as convolution.
claims.quote_verbatim: They have a MCU class and an apps processor class
claims.speaker: Brian Faith
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains and Machine Learning with Brian Faith of QuickLogic

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller and FPGA silicon have converged from both directions: FPGAs gained hard processor blocks and microcontrollers gained small blocks of programmable fabric.
claims.quote_verbatim: the microcontrollers are coming with little embedded sort of, you know, FPGA fabric in them
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller and an FPGA are complementary rather than competing: non-trivial control logic whose timing is not extremely tight is far faster to write as imperative C on a microcontroller than to implement in fabric, which is the argument for pairing the two or instantiating a soft core.
claims.quote_verbatim: it is a lot faster to write imperative code in C or C++ or your favorite language
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: Integration is the practical advantage of a microcontroller over a small FPGA: a PIC handling USB and JTAG programming needs only a 3.3 V regulator and a few decoupling capacitors, whereas small FPGAs typically lack integrated regulators and accurate clocks.
claims.quote_verbatim: the only external devices that it needs is a 3.3 volt regulator and a couple of decoupling capacitors
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: USB requires a clock accuracy that some PIC microcontrollers achieve without a crystal by trimming the internal oscillator on the fly against the synchronisation packets on the USB wires; FPGAs generally lack clock adjustment fine enough to do this and need an external clock.
claims.quote_verbatim: this particular PIC microcontroller can adjust its clock based on the synchronization packets coming over the USB wires
claims.speaker: Luke Valenty

claims.claim_text: An FPGA project is only worth the tooling cost when the task is not easily done on a microcontroller — massively parallel work or hard real-time decoding — rather than tasks such as blinking an LED.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need something that, you know, is not really easily doable on a microcontroller
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Driving LED matrices becomes difficult on a microcontroller quickly because many pins must be driven in parallel with a bit-banged protocol at speed, while an FPGA handles the same job trivially by instantiating parallel units; this makes matrix driving a good first non-trivial FPGA project.
claims.quote_verbatim: driving LED matrices is something that becomes pretty hairy when you use a microcontroller fairly quickly
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: Microcontrollers were unsuitable for logic analyser front ends in the 1990s because they were neither fast enough nor deterministic, which pushed such designs to discrete TTL or early programmable logic.
claims.quote_verbatim: And you can't use a microcontroller. Because microcontrollers aren't. You know. Determined. They're not fast enough
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller and 74HC-series data sheets carry two distinct output-current limits: a maximum per pin, often around 30 mA, and a separate maximum total current through the ground or supply pin, often around 200 mA. A high pin-count part therefore cannot source the per-pin maximum from every pin simultaneously.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will have two specs for output current for each
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Driving a large LED matrix from a single processor fails on bandwidth rather than on drive current: one CPU feeding fifty shift-register modules cannot keep up, so the standard remedy is a local microcontroller per 8x8 tile with the controllers exchanging data.
claims.quote_verbatim: The bandwidth requirements are just so massive that you just can't do it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Directly driving LEDs from microcontroller pins is viable where only a few are lit at a time; at roughly 30 mA per LED with eight on simultaneously the design sits just inside a typical part's maximum total pin current, with a 74HC595 shift register as the alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you've got 30 milliamps per LED, that's probably just within the maximum total pin current specification of the micro
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: LED Designs, Last Minute Designs and Board Designs

claims.claim_text: Vendors rebrand general-purpose microcontrollers as fixed-function parts: the MCP2200 USB-to-serial bridge is a PIC 18F14K50 USB microcontroller carrying preloaded firmware, sold with its own part number, data sheet and qualification.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's an 18F 14K50 USB chip with just some firmware programmed in
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: Some microcontroller peripherals run autonomously without code: a PIC can be configured to sample its analogue-to-digital converter at a fixed period and deposit results in memory with no CPU intervention, which is the same idea as the programmable-peripheral cores appearing in larger parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can actually read a sample from the analog to digital converter and put it into memory
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Where converter timing matters, clocking the ADC and DAC from an external source rather than the microcontroller's own clock generator avoids the jitter that generator introduces.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're clocking in and out samples from the microcontroller with an external clock that's not generated and not subject to the jitter
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Direct memory access controllers give a microcontroller genuine parallelism for communications: a DMA channel configured for a fixed twelve-byte sensor transfer signals a task only when the block is complete, leaving the CPU free for other work throughout the transfer.
claims.quote_verbatim: you set up DMA with a, a transfer block size of 12
claims.speaker: Brian Amos
claims.episode_title: Real Time Operating Systems with Brian Amos

claims.claim_text: A dedicated capacitive touch controller such as the Tontek TTP223 in a six-pin SOT-23 costs under ten cents, offers sensitivity adjustable from about 1 pF to 50 pF, self-calibrates at power-up and emits a debounced, polarity-selectable output that can drive an ordinary microcontroller input or a wake-up interrupt, removing the need for touch peripherals or capacitive-sensing firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: adjustable sensitivity from one picofarad to 50
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Microcontrollers reached USB self-sufficiency in stages: parts arrived with USB hardware and enumeration handled on chip, then with USB bootloaders preloaded so only D+ and D- need connecting. A sufficiently fast core can even bit-bang low-speed USB with no transceiver at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: The actual micro is fast enough to bit bang the original USB
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A field-updatable product needs a bootloader that resides in Flash, runs first at power-up, validates the application image and only then transfers execution; updating requires a documented path back into the bootloader and any communications channel — CAN, USB or a plain UART — capable of carrying the new image.
claims.quote_verbatim: normally what the bootloader does is it checks the application for validity
claims.speaker: Trey German
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Trey German - Launchpad Laden Lodesman

claims.claim_text: Over-the-air update pushes the network stack into the bootloader, and many microcontrollers physically constrain the bootloader region: the space is fixed rather than arbitrary, so a 64 KB part cannot simply be given a 32 KB bootloader containing a Wi-Fi stack.
claims.quote_verbatim: some sections of micros, right. Only have limited bootloader space, physical space

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller program Flash is typically specified for only around ten thousand write cycles because a program memory is expected to be written a handful of times in the device's life, unlike a data EEPROM.
claims.quote_verbatim: how many times do you have to reprogram your microcontroller? Not many, right?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Silicon errata are a routine input to microcontroller selection rather than an exception: a family's errata list will contain defects marked fixed in a later silicon stepping and a substantial number marked with no fix at all, meaning an advertised feature simply does not work.
claims.quote_verbatim: Go and look them up. Look it up all the issues and bugs that will be in the chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: The honest figure of merit for microcontroller power is energy per instruction rather than current per megahertz, because one part may execute an instruction per clock and another one per four clocks; power per MIPS is better still, but data sheets do not publish it.
claims.quote_verbatim: So it should be microwatts per megahertz or microwatts per MIPS
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: At least my house isn't haunted

claims.claim_text: Comparing the power of two microcontrollers is complicated by their internal supply architecture: a core running at 1.2 V behind an internal linear regulator draws roughly constant current, so its power falls as the battery discharges, whereas a part using an internal or external switching converter draws roughly constant power. The only sound comparison is to build both boards, run identical software and exercise every peripheral and sleep mode.
claims.quote_verbatim: really the only way to genuinely compare two micros is to actually build them up
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: At least my house isn't haunted

claims.claim_text: The most effective low-power firmware strategy is to keep the active period short rather than to micro-manage clock trees: wake, complete the task immediately, and sleep, avoiding any state in which the microcontroller is awake waiting on a sensor.
claims.quote_verbatim: you want to have the firmware turn on, do its task, and go back to sleep
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Not every peripheral offers a low-power mode reachable over its control bus, so the fallback is a load switch cutting supply to that subsystem entirely; this in turn creates a back-powering hazard through the signal lines into the unpowered part.
claims.quote_verbatim: you shut the whole thing down, but now you have to worry about back-powering it
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Bulk or off-brand bypass capacitors can carry enough leakage to dominate a low-power design's sleep current, so capacitor selection is a power-budget item and not only a decoupling one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they've had major leakage problems for people that are doing low power design
claims.speaker: Matt Liberty

claims.claim_text: Measuring the current of a connected microcontroller is difficult because of dynamic range: sleep currents and transmit-burst currents can differ by several orders of magnitude within one duty cycle.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you have a large dynamic range of like sleep currents and then large like a transmit current
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Running bare-metal code out of internal SRAM, with no external DRAM, gives a microcontroller sleep-mode power consumption orders of magnitude better than an embedded Linux system, which is the main reason to stay below the Linux threshold.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're using internal SRAM
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: The decision to use an application processor rather than a microcontroller is usually driven by wanting an operating system, a large graphical display and networking, not by raw compute.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're probably choosing arm processor because you want to run a, yeah. And operating system
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Let's Hear It For The Buoys - Vanishing Vessel Vexation

claims.claim_text: Choosing a microcontroller over a Cortex-A application processor for a wearable platform is a power decision, even where third-party application support argues for the larger part; an early product ran a Bluetooth stack on an NXP ARM7 with 32 KB of Flash and a few kilobytes of RAM.
claims.quote_verbatim: choosing a microcontroller as opposed to, um, like an ARM Cortex A microprocessor
claims.speaker: Andrew Witte
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Andrew Witte - Telistic Timepiece Technomania

claims.claim_text: A common early partitioning question is whether the product is a computer platform with a camera and display, in which case a Linux-capable processor and a compute-module prototype follow, or a node doing sensing and control, in which case a microcontroller does. The fact that a part such as an ESP32 can drive a camera and display does not mean it should.
claims.quote_verbatim: Doesn't mean it should be doing that though, just because it can handle the data processing
claims.episode_title: Moving Down The Stack with Scott Williams

claims.claim_text: Embedded GUI toolkits distort the microcontroller-versus-Linux decision: free toolkits are workable but poor-looking, while commercial ones cost around ten thousand dollars in licence fees, which is significant against a low-volume product's margins.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're going to pay 10 K for a license
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Hybrid parts blur the boundary: an STM32MP1 carries a Cortex-M4 with the peripheral set of a top-end STM32H7 — around twenty-two communication peripherals plus timers and ADCs — alongside two 800 MHz Cortex-A7 cores capable of running Linux.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's got literally, it's, it's got the peripheral set that matches the highest end STM 32 H7
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Development boards can silently remove the capability that motivated the part: on one embedded Linux board the parallel LCD pins were routed to an HDMI transmitter, and only a subset of the device's I/O was brought out to any pin at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't even hook up a parallel LCD to this thing
claims.speaker: Jay Carlson

claims.claim_text: Free choice among microcontrollers is a cost, not a benefit, in a working design: an externally imposed constraint to reuse the part already in another product removes a week of comparison with little loss.
claims.quote_verbatim: I don't have to spend a week agonizing over which bloody microcontroller to use
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Project Management, Lasers & Robots - Staunch Specialty Sanctanimity

claims.claim_text: Selecting a microcontroller by parametric search for the cheapest part meeting the requirement, without regard to vendor, is a defensible strategy where the design does not depend on ecosystem or peripheral idiosyncrasies.
claims.quote_verbatim: I go through my parametric search, which is the cheapest brand that'll do that?
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang - Bunnie's Bibelot Bonification

claims.claim_text: Ease of use for a microcontroller is best measured by the breadth of open-source software support — a Zephyr port, a Renode model — rather than by vendor marketing, because a vendor-only toolchain behind an NDA imposes an ongoing cost and no escape route.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ease of use, I think, should be measured in how much open source software is available for this MCU
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: System Designer Lets You Try Every Part with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Substituting within a microcontroller family during a shortage is rarely a drop-in: a single letter's difference in the part number can halve the memory and the peripheral count and change the package, forcing a board respin, a firmware rewrite and a re-partitioning of the system.
claims.quote_verbatim: one letter change and it's like, okay, now you're at half the memory
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Underestimating Flash requirements is a common and expensive error: a design budgeted at 32 KB that could not fit a USB Power Delivery stack had to move to a 128 KB part which was not footprint compatible, forcing an adapter from a TSSOP to a larger quad flat pack and, because of the mechanical space available, a flexible rather than rigid board.
claims.quote_verbatim: we underestimated what we, the amount of space we will require in our microcontroller
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Commoditised, multi-source footprints exist for 74-series logic but not for microcontrollers or switching regulators, so a microcontroller footprint effectively locks a board to one vendor's part.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't do that with like switching regulators and microcontrollers and stuff like that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Radio modules almost always contain their own microcontroller, so a design that wants to run all software on a separate host processor and use only the transceiver has a much smaller module choice and may be pushed to a chip-down implementation.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the modules have an MCU built in
claims.speaker: Ariel Briner

claims.claim_text: Debugging aids consume the resource that is scarcest: printf output over a serial terminal costs a couple of kilobytes on a part whose memory is measured in tens or hundreds of kilobytes rather than megabytes.
claims.quote_verbatim: But, but is it worth a couple of K

claims.claim_text: Pin-multiplexing options are poorly expressible in schematic capture: a net on a microcontroller may legally connect to any of several pins, but only in particular permutations, and CAD tools generally cannot represent that constraint.
claims.quote_verbatim: You can say on your schematic, this node can go to any of these pins
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Harrison - X-ray Examining Xenogogue

claims.claim_text: Bringing up a new microcontroller costs a couple of weeks of work to move smoothly between its interfaces and to learn its internals and limitations, which is a real schedule item rather than a formality.
claims.quote_verbatim: It takes a couple of weeks, you know, to, you know, smoothly go from one interface to other
claims.speaker: Pallav Aggarwal

claims.claim_text: Learning one microcontroller family deeply is transferable capital: six months spent on one Kinetis part made porting a core operating system to any other member of the line a sub-day exercise.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can now port to, like, any, like, target member of that line within, like, less than a day
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: Cheap microcontrollers have moved processing across isolation barriers: rather than routing many analogue converters back to a single processor across an isolator, designs now place a microcontroller on the isolated side and send digital data across.
claims.quote_verbatim: Now you just throw a micro on the other side too
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: Analogue vendors increasingly integrate a microcontroller alongside converters, which forces a designer who wanted only a converter to program the embedded core rather than simply talk to the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: if I'm trying to use it just as an analog to digital converter, then I have to go and program that micro
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Contextual Electronics, ClubJameco and Solderpaste - Lifelong Learning Likelihood

claims.claim_text: Per-cell battery monitoring can be built by giving each cell its own microcontroller powered from that cell, using the part's internal ADC and voltage reference, with an optocoupler carrying serial data out of the cell's floating voltage domain.
claims.quote_verbatim: So each cell would have a little microcontroller, I presume using the built-in ADC and a voltage reference and then an optocoupler to shoot the serial data out
claims.speaker: Bob Simpson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bob Simpson - Ardent Automotive Artisan

claims.claim_text: Where extra conductors are prohibitively expensive — such as sixty feet of cabling in an electronic drum kit — control data can be carried as a modulated high-frequency carrier superimposed on the existing 12 V DC supply and demodulated by a microcontroller at each end point.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I just superimposed some modulated high frequency carrier on the 12 volt DC supply
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Industrial 24 V I/O is interfaced to a 3.3 V or 5 V microcontroller through optocouplers: the input side takes the 24 V loop and the open-collector output provides a low-voltage, low-current signal, with the arrangement reversed on the outputs and a triac driven through the optocoupler for AC loads.
claims.quote_verbatim: you got 24 volts. Well, you know, the poor microcontroller is five volt or 3.3 volt compliant. It can't handle that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Engineering Education with Dr Don Wilcher

claims.claim_text: Opto-isolated CAN transceivers exist specifically to separate the microcontroller from the bus; more generally, bus drivers serve both to isolate and to supply the current needed to drive the line capacitance.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get a opto isolated, uh, yeah. Driver chip that isolates your microcontroller from the bus
claims.speaker: Joris Aerts
claims.episode_title: Satellites and EVs with Joris Aerts

claims.claim_text: Sampling oscilloscope bandwidth is set entirely by the front-end sample-and-hold, so once a sample is captured the conversion can be arbitrarily slow; a design achieving multi-gigahertz front-end bandwidth can use the ADC inside an inexpensive PIC microcontroller to digitise the held value.
claims.quote_verbatim: it just uses a regular PIC microcontroller as the ADC
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A software-defined power supply can close its control loop in firmware if the converter is fast enough: an XMega chosen for a 2 megasample, 12-bit successive-approximation ADC gives a short enough lag between sample, regulation decision and DAC or PWM output to regulate in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: a two mega sample SAR ADC
claims.speaker: Werner Johansson
claims.episode_title: Software Defined Power Supplies with Werner Johansson

claims.claim_text: A direct digital synthesis function generator is architecturally a microcontroller issuing SPI commands to a DDS chip such as the AD9837, with the DDS setting output frequency from DC up to its own limit; the microcontroller adds no signal path.
claims.quote_verbatim: You basically have a microcontroller, which sends in the spy commands into the analog devices, DDS chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Pin count, not compute, often drives the microcontroller choice in display designs: driving thirty-two segments plus eight commons requires at least forty dedicated pins, and the larger package that offers them comes with a larger die and far more memory, tripling the chip price. An external LCD driver on an SPI bus is then cheaper, and also lets the display driver and the microcontroller sit on opposite sides of the board, easing layout and signal integrity.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got at least 40 pins dedicated to the lcd
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Moving a function into a dedicated external chip to save microcontroller pins or memory adds a BOM line that can go obsolete or become unobtainable, and a part that is not stocked at ordinary distributors must be bought in quantity from a distributor with no substitute available if it disappears.
claims.quote_verbatim: then you've got another bomb item right and then you've got another thing that could go obsolete
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Partitioning between chip and board turns on confidence: blocks that are proven and would add another supply or another failure domain go on-chip, while anything whose behaviour is still uncertain — particularly firmware-controlled functions — goes on a microcontroller next to the chip with a bus between them.
claims.quote_verbatim: then we'll put the microcontroller on the board next door and run a bus
claims.speaker: Adrian Tang

claims.claim_text: A microcontroller can replace substantial amounts of discrete logic outright: designs requiring twenty to thirty 74-series packages collapse into a single small part costing a few cents, though the discrete version remains the better teaching example for timing-critical pin driving.
claims.quote_verbatim: I can shrink those 20, uh, TTL chips into one three cent micro
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Logic probes fell out of use because they cannot be applied to microcontroller-based designs; they worked when a board was discrete logic in DIP packages that could be probed pin by pin against a schematic.
claims.quote_verbatim: the reason logic probes died is because you can't use them on microcontrollers
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: An interactive bus tool that sends protocol transactions from a terminal removes the edit-compile-program-test loop when learning an unfamiliar chip, and isolates whether a fault lies in the protocol, the chip or the wiring.
claims.quote_verbatim: That helps you avoid that development cycle where you write some code, program it to your microcontroller
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: A modern car is a network of interconnected computers with a microcontroller in each subsystem, which makes the attack pattern the same as a corporate network: compromise any one node, including a peripheral one such as a tyre-pressure sensor, and use it as a foothold onto the shared bus.
claims.quote_verbatim: every single little subsystem in the car has its own microcontroller doing something
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Tyre pressure monitoring systems are of particular security interest because each of the four sensors independently and periodically transmits a radio signal to a central controller, putting identifiable data outside the vehicle.
claims.quote_verbatim: each one is independently transmitting periodically a radio signal to a centralized controller
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: A Security Update with Michael Ossmann

claims.claim_text: Microcontroller counts per vehicle follow from the bus architecture: a low-end car has around twenty electronic control units, an average car around fifty and a high-end car up to a hundred, and each LIN bus below them carries a further five to ten microcontrollers across several dozen LIN buses, giving totals of the order of five hundred to seven hundred microcontrollers per car.
claims.quote_verbatim: 50 ECUs is probably now around average
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Abstraction layers in automotive firmware carry a direct silicon cost: generated code running four or five times the size of the application forces a larger microcontroller, and multiplied across millions of vehicles a single coding-standard decision can be worth tens of millions of dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: You're talking kind of four or five times the size of the application
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Abstraction is a poorer fit in embedded systems than in general computing because low-level behaviour propagates upward and affects the result, so hiding the hardware hides the things the engineer must know.
claims.quote_verbatim: for embedded systems, you need to know things because they bubble up from the bottom
claims.speaker: Ken Tindell
claims.episode_title: The CAN bus can! with Dr Ken Tindell

claims.claim_text: Encrypting a firmware image with a key pre-programmed into the target microcontroller lets a manufacturer send the binary to a contract assembler anywhere: only devices already holding the key can program it, though the protection is only as strong as the difficulty of extracting the key from the die.
claims.quote_verbatim: that key is on the micros
claims.speaker: Colin O'Flynn
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Colin O'Flynn - Aspirated Adamantine Attacks

claims.claim_text: Firmware extraction is structurally easier on Linux-class devices because their storage is external and can be read with a suitable flash reader; on a microcontroller with internal Flash the attacker's first question is whether the debug interface was left enabled, and where it was locked out, fault injection or glitching the device into a state that divulges the firmware is the remaining route.
claims.quote_verbatim: when there's internal flash on the microcontroller
claims.speaker: Matt Brown

claims.claim_text: A hardware wallet's security model is that the private key stays inside the microcontroller or secure element and never reaches the host: the host sends a transaction, the device displays the details for physical confirmation, performs the ECDSA sign operation internally and returns only the signature.
claims.quote_verbatim: the private key stays in the, uh, memory of the microcontroller or secure element, and it never leaves into the host computer
claims.speaker: Josh Datko

claims.claim_text: Consumables can be limited artificially by firmware: an inkjet cartridge physically capable of 2,500 pages may carry a microcontroller that refuses to print after 500, with no difference in the cartridge itself.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have a microcontroller on there that after 500 pages says, you know what, I can't print
claims.speaker: Dmitry Nedospasov

claims.claim_text: USB-C cables rated above three amps must be electronically marked, meaning a microcontroller in the plug answers a specific packet — a requirement that can be, and is, faked by cables carrying a fraction of the specified copper.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cable itself has to be what's called electronically marked
claims.speaker: Jason Cerundolo

claims.claim_text: Analogue-era mobile phones were built from an 8-bit microcontroller with external ROM, since the code did not fit on chip, plus a serial EEPROM holding the electronic serial number in a standard bit-packed format of country, manufacturer and model codes followed by a sixteen-bit serial number; the ROM images ran to 32 to 64 KB and every manufacturer used a different processor.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'd have an 8-bit microcontroller
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Live from Serbia with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: A productive way into unfamiliar firmware is to locate the code that touches a known I/O pin — for instance the pins wired to an external serial EEPROM — and then work outward through the calls to that routine, which quickly identifies the code handling the data of interest.
claims.quote_verbatim: you look through that code, look for any access to that iopin
claims.speaker: Mike Harrison
claims.episode_title: Live from Serbia with Mike Harrison

claims.claim_text: Consumer instruments frequently expose an undocumented in-circuit programming header for the internal microcontroller, but a rebranded, house-marked part defeats third-party repair because the replacement chip cannot be identified or sourced.
claims.quote_verbatim: you've got to know what micro it is to begin with
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: European CE marking rules have been extended so that essentially any product containing a microcontroller must be field updatable, which rules out designs built on one-time-programmable memory.
claims.quote_verbatim: anything that has a cable on it, anything that's basically electronic or has a microcontroller. You have to be able to update it
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Radiation-induced bit flips make microcontroller-based designs a mission-duration question: for a six-month low-earth-orbit CubeSat the probability of an upset is low, but for a five-year mission in an orbit that will not decay for a decade it is not, particularly where the device cannot be reprogrammed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can get radiation bit flips and, you know, your code can literally change ones and zeros, uh, due to radiation
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: Replacing a microcontroller-based maximum power point tracker with an analogue one eliminates stored state, which is what radiation corrupts: an analogue loop recomputes continuously, so a particle strike produces a transient the feedback corrects, and the failure mode becomes gradual degradation rather than sudden loss.
claims.quote_verbatim: it avoided something called state
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brent and Bryce Salmi

claims.claim_text: A given microcontroller running an interpreted high-level language does roughly an eighth of the work at roughly eight times the execution time, which is the concrete trade being made for development speed.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can do, you know, an eighth of what you could do otherwise. And probably in, in eight times the time
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Getting a Python implementation to run on a microcontroller at all is substantial engineering; MicroPython, created by Damien George, targets a relatively technical audience, and CircuitPython is a derivative retargeted by Adafruit at the Atmel SAM D family with a more hardware-oriented interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting it running on a microcontroller is really hard
claims.speaker: Scott Shawcroft

claims.claim_text: A layered API is what allows a beginner platform to remain useful: an LED can be blinked in about seven lines at the top layer, and a developer who needs finer control can strip a layer and work against a more granular interface on the same hardware.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can blink an LED with, what, seven lines of code
claims.speaker: Massimo Banzi
claims.episode_title: Arduino's Invisible Touch with Massimo Banzi

claims.claim_text: Teaching against a specific microcontroller rather than an abstract model is what transfers: the durable skills are talking to registers, writing legible C, interfacing hardware and debugging hardware through the code written for it, none of which is tied to the part chosen.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're really learning is like how to talk to registers
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A general-purpose programming curriculum still benefits from teaching pointers early through C or C++, because understanding how the microcontroller actually works underpins the rest.
claims.quote_verbatim: understanding how the microcontroller actually works makes everything else useful
claims.speaker: Elecia White

claims.claim_text: Microcontrollers do not remove the need for fundamentals: an on-chip ADC still usually needs an amplifier in front of it, so discrete and gate-level design remain prerequisites rather than superseded knowledge.
claims.quote_verbatim: They've got ADCs built in, but, you know, you need an amplifier on the front end often to do that
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Machine learning on microcontrollers works by splitting the workload: the model is trained on servers and only the resulting inference model is loaded onto the part, so a Cortex-M4 performs inference rather than training.
claims.quote_verbatim: you do all the, the actual value creation
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Video codecs are the limit case for microcontroller compute: without a hardware decoder, decoding H.264, H.265 or AV1 in software is not feasible on a microcontroller, so streaming to such a device requires a lightweight custom compression scheme for simple graphical content.
claims.quote_verbatim: decoding them in software is not feasible, you know, on a microcontroller
claims.speaker: Aedan Cullen
claims.episode_title: Building AR Headsets with Aedan Cullen

claims.claim_text: Precomputing a bit stream on a host and shifting it out of a microcontroller lets a simple part synthesise complex signals it could never compute in real time: the firmware holds only a table and has no representation of the waveform it is producing at 900 MHz.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's just a table that gets produced by the first step and you just shift through it on the microcontroller
claims.speaker: CNLohr

claims.claim_text: Programming and test are separate stations in volume production: a board carrying three microcontrollers and two SPI Flash devices passed through five stations, one per programmable device, before reaching a bed-of-nails self-test fixture and only then final assembly.
claims.quote_verbatim: we actually have three microcontrollers on there
claims.speaker: Jonathan Georgino

claims.claim_text: Distributed motion control can keep multiple microcontrollers in step by moving the scheduler to a host: a Linux process sends timed packets over USB to each microcontroller so that step timing on a moving head stays synchronised with the base.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's actually like something that runs on Linux that does real time, like packet sending over USB to the microcontrollers
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: Microcontrollers made retro and obsolete hardware repairable: a small microcontroller or FPGA can replicate a failed function, which is how emulated SCSI disks, keyboard adapters and similar substitutes for unobtainable subsystems are built.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can build a small microcontroller or FPGA part that replicates the pieces that are no longer functional
claims.speaker: Trammell Hudson

claims.claim_text: Where a chip must be verified as a design rather than as a package, an accelerator ASIC is treated as a slave to a microcontroller: the firmware and the parallel interface between them are brought up against an FPGA port of the same RTL, because the ASIC itself will be about nine months at the fab.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to take nine months for my ASIC to come back from the fab
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Cheap parts with wide internal RC oscillator tolerance can be a feature rather than a defect: a network of ATtiny44A boards each clocked from its own internal RC oscillator ran asynchronously with slightly different timing, which was exactly the behaviour the model required.
claims.quote_verbatim: each one of the boards used the internal RC oscillator of the chip. So each one was a little bit different
claims.speaker: Zach Fredin

claims.claim_text: Frequency hopping across a span wider than the receiver's instantaneous bandwidth must be implemented in the microcontroller firmware rather than commanded from the host, because USB latency added to the roughly hundred-microsecond retune time exceeds the gap between packets — a little over 200 microseconds in Bluetooth, which itself spans 79 MHz against a 20 MHz instantaneous bandwidth.
claims.quote_verbatim: you'll probably need to implement your frequency hopping in the microcontroller
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Before dedicated microcontrollers, some functions were served by proto-microcontrollers: sound playback chips with no logic at all, configured by a paper form specifying trigger behaviour, evolving into rudimentary state machines that were only generously described as programmable.
claims.quote_verbatim: they were sort of proto microcontrollers
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: A CPLD containing small SRAM blocks — 256 by 8 in one early part — was enough to implement a microcontroller with its program stored inside the same chip, a capability no other programmable logic of the era offered and the direct ancestor of soft cores in FPGAs.
claims.quote_verbatim: you could actually make a little microcontroller out of that chip and store the programs inside
claims.speaker: Dave Vandenbout
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Dave Vandenbout - Xceptional XESS Xenagogue

name: Microcontroller
